summary.text: The Milky Way is the galaxy that contains the Solar System, named for the hazy band of light it makes across the night sky.
Its innermost stars form a bulge from which a bar radiates, which makes it a barred spiral galaxy.
Until the early 1920s most astronomers thought it held every star in the universe, until Hubble's observations in 1923 showed it is one of many galaxies.

facts.label: Sun's position

facts.label: Resolved into stars
facts.value: Galileo did it with a telescope in 1610

items.prompt: On a dark night you see a pale, hazy stripe across the sky instead of separate points of light. Why does it look hazy?

options.label: The stripe is a thin cloud of gas lit by moonlight
Its stars are so far off that the naked eye cannot separate them
Its stars are too dim to give off any light at all
The stripe is a glow from Earth's own atmosphere

items.explain: The band is formed by stars so far away that the naked eye cannot tell them apart.

items.prompt: Until the early 1920s, most astronomers pictured the universe as nothing beyond our own star system. What changed their minds?

options.label: Observations showed that ours is just one of many galaxies
Astronomers counted every star and found far fewer than expected
Telescopes revealed the hazy band to be a cloud of gas
A search found a huge region of unseen matter around our system

items.explain: Edwin Hubble's observations in 1923 showed the Milky Way was just one of many galaxies.

items.prompt: Picture our galaxy as a giant pinwheel of stars. Roughly where does the Sun sit in it?

options.label: At the very center, next to the black hole
In the central bulge, packed among the oldest stars
On the inner edge of one arm, far out from the center
Outside the pinwheel, in the surrounding dark matter

items.explain: The Solar System sits on the inner edge of the Orion Arm, about 27,000 light-years from the Galactic Center.

items.prompt: Astronomers detect an intense radio signal from the exact middle of our galaxy. What is the object producing it?

options.label: A single star many times larger than the Sun
A dense cluster of the galaxy's oldest stars
A vast cloud of dark matter with no compact core
A supermassive black hole named Sagittarius A*

items.explain: At the center is an intense radio source known as Sagittarius A*, a supermassive black hole.

items.prompt: At high northern latitudes in midsummer, the band of light is hard to spot. What gets in the way?

options.label: Warm summer air scatters starlight away from the band
Stars in the summer sky are fainter than in winter
The Sun's glow late at night can wash it out
The galaxy itself fades during the summer months

items.explain: Swedes call it Winter Street because it is clearest in winter, while in summer the Sun's glow late at night can obscure it.

items.prompt: Some patches inside the glowing band look dark. What explains them?

options.label: Empty gaps where the galaxy has no stars at all
Black holes swallowing the light of stars behind them
Areas where interstellar dust blocks light from distant stars
Shadows cast by the Moon across the band

items.explain: Dark regions such as the Great Rift and the Coalsack are areas where interstellar dust blocks light from distant stars.
